headline: Film-Grade Ocean Simulation Comes to the Browser via WebGPU
lede: Three.js Water Pro is a commercial ocean-rendering asset that brings the kind of wave physics found in film VFX and console games into the browser — through WebGPU, the modern successor to WebGL. Dan Greenheck opened a public demo at threejswaterpro.com as version 2.1 shipped, inviting visitors to stress-test it on their own hardware. The timing is deliberate: Apple (AAPL) shipped WebGPU support in Safari 26 in September 2025, completing universal browser coverage and opening a production market for GPU-native web assets for the first time.
body:
The gap Three.js Water Pro fills is genuine. The water addons bundled with Three.js — the dominant JavaScript 3D library — are decorative rather than physically grounded. The standard `Water` class renders a flat reflective plane shimmered by a looping normal map; `Water2` adds animation through *flow maps* but provides no wave-height displacement and exhibits documented artifacts at low camera angles. Three.js Water Pro replaces both with a full simulation stack: two *FFT* (fast Fourier transform) ocean cascades driven by the *JONSWAP* spectrum — a wave-growth model developed for offshore engineering — layered with *Gerstner swells* for large open-ocean rollers. A three-layer foam system covers whitecapping crests, ambient surface foam, and shoreline contact; the surface adds physically-based *Fresnel* reflections, *screen-space reflections (SSR)*, caustics, and subsurface scattering through wave crests.

The underlying engine is **WebGPU**, which exposes compute shaders — general-purpose GPU programs — to browser code. Three.js Water Pro runs its FFT wave evaluation as a GPU compute pass each frame, work that would overwhelm the CPU if executed in software. Shaders are written in *TSL* (Three Shading Language), Three.js's JavaScript-based shader composition layer that compiles a single description to both WGSL (for WebGPU) and GLSL (for WebGL), so the asset operates on both renderers without duplicated code. Geometry uses a *geometry clipmap* — concentric rings of progressively coarser mesh — to concentrate vertex density near the camera while keeping the horizon affordable.

Greenheck is primarily known as an open-source contributor: *ez-tree*, his procedural tree generator, has accumulated over 1,300 GitHub stars, and *OpenFracture*, a real-time mesh-slicing library, crossed 1,100 stars on Unity before he ported the concept to Three.js. Three.js Water Pro is his first significant paid asset, sold as a one-time purchase through threejsroadmap.com, a platform he is building into a broader Three.js course ecosystem. Version 2.0 launched in March 2026; v2.1 followed quickly, delivering roughly 30 percent faster frame rates across quality presets.

The demo's prominent performance counters — GPU load, draw count, *DPR* (device pixel ratio, which governs rendering resolution on high-density displays) — signal a deliberate design philosophy. WebGPU's compute path is fast, but ocean simulation remains genuinely expensive; users on mobile or integrated graphics face real trade-offs. Greenheck built preset tiers ("Choppy" through "Ultra") alongside granular per-parameter controls precisely to surface those limits. The live demo functions as diagnostic instrument as much as product showcase.

concepts.definition: The modern browser graphics API, successor to WebGL. Unlike WebGL, WebGPU exposes compute shaders — general-purpose GPU programs — allowing simulation-heavy workloads like FFT ocean evaluation to run entirely on the GPU. Achieved universal browser support when Apple shipped it in Safari 26 in September 2025.

The browser graphics API based on OpenGL ES, dominant from roughly 2011 to 2024. WebGL enables GPU-accelerated 3D rendering in the browser but lacks compute shader support, limiting simulation-heavy workloads. Three.js Water Pro targets WebGPU but falls back to WebGL 2 automatically.

A technique for simulating ocean wave fields using the fast Fourier transform. Wave spectra are defined in the frequency domain — describing which wavelengths and directions carry energy — then an inverse FFT converts them to spatial wave-height maps each frame. Used in industrial VFX tools like Houdini and AAA game engines; Three.js Water Pro brings the same approach to browser WebGPU.

Joint North Sea Wave Project — a physics-based model of how ocean waves grow under sustained wind, derived from field measurements in the North Sea. It encodes the relationship between wind speed, fetch (how far the wind has blown over open water), and the resulting wave energy distribution across frequencies. Using JONSWAP as the input to an FFT simulation produces physically plausible wind-driven seas.

A family of analytical wave solutions in which water particles trace circular orbits, producing the characteristic rolling shape of open-ocean swells. Computationally cheap compared to FFT and useful for adding large, non-tiling waves on top of a simulated chop field. Three.js Water Pro layers Gerstner swells over its FFT cascades to break up repetitive tiling at ocean scale.

Textures that encode 2D velocity vectors, used to animate a water surface by distorting a repeating normal map in the direction the water is flowing. Cheap and visually convincing for rivers and calm pools but produce no actual wave-height geometry, making them unsuitable for open-ocean or surf simulation.

The optical phenomenon where a surface's reflectivity increases as the viewing angle becomes shallower. Water viewed straight down is mostly transparent; water at a grazing angle is almost mirror-like. Correct Fresnel treatment is a baseline requirement for physically-based water shading.

A real-time rendering technique that approximates reflections by ray-marching within the 2D pixel buffer of the current frame, rather than re-rendering the scene from a reflected camera. Cheaper than true reflections and convincing for water surfaces, but limited to objects currently visible on-screen — off-screen objects cannot be reflected.

Three.js's JavaScript-based shader composition system, introduced alongside the WebGPU renderer. Developers express shader logic as JavaScript function trees; the compiler emits WGSL for WebGPU and GLSL for WebGL from the same source. TSL makes it practical to maintain a single complex shader codebase that runs across both graphics APIs.

A level-of-detail technique for rendering infinite terrains or water surfaces. Multiple concentric rings of mesh surround the camera, each ring twice as coarse as the one inside it; as the camera moves, rings update so vertex density is always concentrated near the viewer. The result is a seamless infinite surface without the cost of uniformly dense geometry to the horizon.

The ratio of a device's physical screen pixels to its logical CSS pixels. A Retina display has DPR 2, meaning a 400×300 CSS element actually renders at 800×600. For GPU-intensive WebGPU work, DPR is a key performance lever: halving it on a high-DPR screen roughly quarters the pixel fill cost.

repos.summary: A procedural tree generator written in JavaScript/Three.js with over 1,300 GitHub stars. Users specify parameters — species, branch density, wind — and get a realistic 3D tree mesh, exportable or live in a Three.js scene. It established Greenheck's reputation in the Three.js open-source community before he moved into commercial tooling.

A real-time mesh fracturing and slicing library originally written for Unity (C#), with over 1,100 GitHub stars. It computes Voronoi-based fracture geometry at runtime, enabling destructible objects without pre-authored break states. Greenheck later ported the concept to Three.js as the library three-pinata.
